title: Classical Education Has a Machiavelli Problem
author: Benjamin V. Beier
summary: Benjamin V. Beier, an education professor at Hillsdale College, argues that Machiavelli has increasingly been held up within classical education circles as an exemplum -- a figure whose life and thought students are meant to admire and imitate -- and that this move is a genuine error rather than a defensible pedagogical choice. Beier first establishes the medieval and classical pedagogical logic of the exemplum, noting that even flawed historical figures (Washington, Thomas More, Martin Luther King Jr.) can rightly serve this role when educators tell the truth about both their virtues and their faults, but argues Machiavelli fails a different test: influence and curricular importance do not equal the sapience or virtue required of an exemplum. Drawing on both the popular reputation of Machiavelli as a byword for amoral cunning and a close reading of The Prince and The Discourses, Beier contends that Machiavelli redefines virtù to include cruelty and violence, subverts Christian theological virtue, and places worldly power above authentic human flourishing -- placing him fundamentally against, not within, the humanist classical education tradition. The essay closes by critically examining two recent essays (by Matthew Freeman and Henry Olsen) that use Machiavellian ideas or figures within classical education discourse, arguing both problematically narrow the movement's concern to an ambitious "few" and conflate ambition for victory with genuine virtuous ambition.
points: Beier distinguishes between teaching Machiavelli as curricular content (which he endorses) and holding him up as an exemplum -- a figure whose character students are meant to imitate -- arguing influence and novelty do not equal the virtue an exemplum requires.

His close reading of The Prince and The Discourses argues Machiavelli deliberately redefines virtù to include cruelty, violence, and victory in place of the Aristotelian and Ciceronian cardinal virtues, and inverts Christian theological virtues into weaknesses.

Beier critiques Matthew Freeman's 2023 essay for constructing an implicitly Machiavellian "canon of thugs" (Achilles, Romulus, Caesar alongside Jesus and Socrates) meant to be "worshiped" by an excellent few, arguing this misreads figures like Christ and Achilles and amounts to indoctrination in brutality rather than classical education.

Against Henry Olsen's more nuanced attempt to adapt Machiavellian leadership attributes for democratic figures like Lincoln and FDR, Beier argues contemporary classical education must be concerned with both the talented few and the broader all, including students with disabilities, not exclusively an ambitious elite.

The essay's central distinction -- ambition for victory and fame versus ambition for virtue -- gives classical educators a specific conceptual tool for critiquing Machiavellian pedagogical frameworks without dismissing engagement with Machiavelli's thought altogether.
quotes: This essay is ultimately interested in whether or not the figure of Machiavelli can serve as a fitting exemplum and auctor for the project of contemporary classical education, but before addressing that matter directly, it is necessary to say a bit more about classical education and exempla in general.

To be clear, I do not object to teaching Machiavelli in classical education. This revolutionary and influential figure must be in curricula. However, influence and novelty do not equal the sapience, virtue, or artistic excellence requisite for a figure to serve as a fitting exemplum.

With revolutionary intent, Machiavelli boldly but wrongly redefines excellence (virtù) to include attributes like cruelty, violence, and victory rather than the excellences of the cardinal virtues as understood by Aristotle and Cicero. He subverts Christianity and makes the theological virtues into weaknesses.

Rather than explicitly offer Machiavelli as an exemplum, Freeman - without credit to the Italian - admires and wishes to inculcate a Machiavellian virtù. The result is a canon of thugs (with at least Jesus and Socrates dubiously canonized).

The Machiavellian frame that Olsen deploys suggests a problematic conflation of ambition for victory (gratification, fame, "greatness") and ambition for virtue (and virtuous achievement), and lacks the resources to distinguish between a settled affection of holy ambition and its counterfeit.

As we begin a new school year, may classical and liberal educators foreswear Machiavelli and rediscover and employ with honesty and piety those examples who actually capture the beauty of our noble activity.
